1:1: Here the phrase according to could indicate: (1) that the purpose for which Paul is an apostle is to tell others about the promise of life; (2) that the reason why Paul is an apostle is the promise of life; (3) that God’s will contains or includes the promise of life.
Here Paul uses the spatial metaphor in Christ Jesus to describe life that can only be experienced when someone is in union with Christ Jesus.
Here Paul is referring to new, eternal life with God.
1:2: Paul speaks of his close relationship to Timothy as though Timothy were his beloved child. Paul means that he considers himself to be Timothy’s spiritual father, and Paul loves Timothy in the way a father loves his child.
After stating his name and the name of the person to whom he is writing, Paul adds a blessing for Timothy.
Father is an important title for God the Father that describes his relationship with Jesus his Son.
1:3: Here Paul means that he serves God in the same way that his ancestors did.
A conscience that is pure is one that does not convict a person of doing anything wrong.
Here the phrase night and day indicates that Paul prays during both the night and the day. This means that he was praying very often every day.
1:4: Here Paul implies that Timothy shed tears when Paul had to leave Timothy.
Here the word tears represents the act of shedding tears, that is, crying.
Paul speaks of himself as if he were a container that could be filled with joy. He means that he will experience very much joy.
1:5: Here Paul speaks as if faith were a living thing that could be or dwell in some location. In this context, he means that Timothy, Lois, and Eunice all have faith.
Paul does not indicate whether this grandmother is the mother of Timothy’s father or mother.
The words Lois and Eunice are the names of women.
1:6: Here the phrase which reason refers back to the fact of Timothy’s sincere faith (see 1:5).

Here Paul speaks of Timothy’s gift as if it were a fire that he needed to rekindle. He could mean that: (1) Timothy needs to use his gift more than he has in the past; (2) Timothy needs to start using his gift again, with the implication being that he has stopped using it consistently.
τὸ χάρισμα τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὅ ἐστιν ἐν σοὶ
Paul speaks of Timothy as if he were a container that could hold the gift of God. He means that Timothy has this gift.
τὸ χάρισμα τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὅ ἐστιν ἐν σοὶ
Here Paul implies that this gift is a specific ability or skill that God had given Timothy for his ministry.
διὰ τῆς ἐπιθέσεως τῶν χειρῶν μου
Here Paul is speaking of a ceremony during which he put his hands on Timothy. When he did that, he was commissioning Timothy to use his gift and to proclaim the gospel.
1:7: πνεῦμα δειλίας, ἀλλὰ δυνάμεως, καὶ ἀγάπης, καὶ σωφρονισμοῦ
Here the word spirit could refer to: (1) the spirit of a person, meaning the inner life of a person, that is, how that person thinks, feels, and makes decisions; (2) the Holy Spirit.
Here the word self-control could refer to: (1) the ability to control or restrain one’s desires; (2) the ability to make wise decisions.
1:8: Here the phrase suffer together could indicate that Timothy should suffer with: (1) Paul; (2) all Christians who suffer.
Here Paul implies that Timothy should be willing to suffer as he believes in and proclaims the gospel.
1:9: Here the phrase holy calling could refer to: (1) the result of being called, which is to be holy; (2) the way in which God called, which is a holy way.
ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων

Here Paul uses the spatial metaphor in Christ Jesus to describe the union of believers with Christ Jesus. In this case, being in Christ Jesus, or united to Christ, is the only way in which believers are given grace.
Here Paul is indicating that God did this before God made the world and before time began to be counted.
1:10: διὰ τῆς ἐπιφανείας τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν, Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ
Here the word appearance refers to when Jesus became a human being, lived on earth, died, and rose again.
φωτίσαντος δὲ ζωὴν καὶ ἀφθαρσίαν διὰ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου
Here Paul speaks as if Jesus used the gospel to shine a light on life and immortality. He means that, by using the gospel, Jesus revealed how people can have life and immortality.
The two words life and immortality express a single idea. The word immortality describes what kind of life Paul is speaking about.
Here Paul is referring to new, eternal life with God.
1:11: A herald is someone who is sent out to announce a message.
1:12: Here the phrase which reason refers back to the fact that Paul was appointed to be a herald, apostle, and teacher (see 1:11).
Here Paul does not mention the specific things that he is suffering, but from the context of the letter, Timothy would have known that he was referring to suffering as a prisoner (see 2:9).

Here Paul speaks as if God were guarding a deposit of money or goods. He means that God will protect or preserve the deposit. What the deposit represents depends on what you chose in the previous note about who gave the deposit to whom. If the deposit: (1) was given by Paul to God, then it could represent Paul himself, the rewards he will receive, or his resurrection life; (2) was given by God to Paul, then it could represent the gospel or Paul’s ministry.
Here Paul is referring to the exact moment when Jesus will return to this world, which will also be the end of the current time period.
1:13: Here Paul indicates that he wants Timothy to maintain the basic form and content of the healthy words.
Here Paul speaks as if words could be healthy. He means that these words are good and reliable in every way and have no defect or corruption.
Here, the word words represents things spoken using words.
Here, the phrase in Christ Jesus could describe: (1) both faith and love; (2) just love.

Paul uses the spatial metaphor in Christ Jesus to describe the union of believers with Christ. In this case, being in Christ Jesus, or united to Christ Jesus, explains how Timothy can have faith and love.
1:14: Here, the phrase good deposit refers to something that has been entrusted to Timothy and that he must Guard. More specifically, the good deposit is the gospel, which God entrusted to Timothy.
Here Paul speaks as if believers were buildings and as if the Holy Spirit were dwelling in them. He means that the Holy Spirit is with believers in a special way and empowers them.
1:15: Paul says all here as an overstatement to emphasize how many believers turned away from him.
Here the phrase the ones in Asia could refer to: (1) believers who are living in Asia; (2) believers who are from Asia but who were with Paul where he was imprisoned, which was probably in Rome.
Here Paul speaks of people who stopped listening to him and helping him as if they had turned away from him.
Here Paul implies that these people turned away because Paul was accused of doing what was wrong, and he was put in jail.
The words Phygelus and Hermogenes are the names of men.
1:16: δῴη ἔλεος ὁ Κύριος τῷ Ὀνησιφόρου οἴκῳ
Here Paul asks God to bless the family of Onesiphorus.
The word Onesiphorus is the name of a man.
Here, chain represents imprisonment or being in jail.
1:17: Here Paul implies that he was in prison in Rome.
1:18: δῴη αὐτῷ ὁ Κύριος, εὑρεῖν ἔλεος παρὰ Κυρίου
Here Paul again asks God to bless Onesiphorus.
Here Paul speaks of mercy as if it were an object that Onesiphorus could find. He means that he wants Onesiphorus to experience mercy.
Here Paul is referring to the exact moment when Jesus will return to this world, which will also be when he judges everyone.
Here Paul could be implying that Onesiphorus served: (1) Paul specifically; (2) believers in general.
2:1: Paul speaks of his close relationship to Timothy as though Timothy were his child. Paul means that he is Timothy’s spiritual father, and Paul loves Timothy in the way a father loves his child.
Here the word in could introduce: (1) the circumstance in which Timothy is strengthened; (2) the means by which Timothy is strengthened.

Here Paul uses the spatial metaphor in Christ Jesus to describe the union of believers with Christ Jesus. In this case, being in Christ Jesus, or united to Christ Jesus, is the way in which Timothy is given grace.
2:2: Here the phrase through many witnesses could indicate that: (1) many people have witnessed or testified to the truth of what Paul has taught Timothy; (2) Timothy has been taught by Paul in the presence of many people who can witness or testify to what Paul said.

Paul speaks of his teachings as if they were objects that Timothy could physically place before other people. He means that Timothy should give these people the same teachings that Paul gave to Timothy.
2:3: Here the phrase Suffer together could indicate that Timothy should suffer with: (1) Paul; (2) all Christians who suffer.

Here Paul speaks as if Timothy were a soldier who fights for and serves Jesus Christ. A good soldier is one who obeys his commander even if that means suffering and pain. So, Timothy will be like a good soldier when he obeys Jesus even if that means that he will Suffer together with Paul.
2:4: Here Paul continues to speak about a soldier to help Timothy understand how to behave. Just as a soldier focuses on pleasing his commander, so Timothy should focus on pleasing Jesus. To do so, he will have to avoid becoming entangled in the affairs of life.

Paul speaks of the affairs of life as if they were a net that could trap people and keep them from being able to move freely. He means that the affairs of life would prevent a soldier from doing what he is supposed to do.
Here the phrase the affairs of life refers to the normal things that people who are not soldiers do and care about, including having a job and owning a home.
2:5: Here Paul speaks about an athlete who competes in a sport. He speaks about this to help Timothy understand how to behave. Just as an athlete will only receive the crown given to the winner if he competes lawfully, so Timothy will only be rewarded if he serves Jesus lawfully, that is, as Jesus desires.
Here Paul uses an imaginary situation to show what happens when athletes do not compete lawfully.
Here the word competes refers specifically to competing in an athletic event.
In Paul’s culture, when athletes won competitions, they were crowned with wreaths made from the leaves of plants.
Here Paul refers to the rules that governed a competition. The athletes had to obey the rules, or they would be removed from the competition and not have an opportunity to win.
2:6: τὸν κοπιῶντα γεωργὸν δεῖ πρῶτον τῶν καρπῶν μεταλαμβάνειν

Here Paul speaks about a farmer who is hardworking. He speaks about this to help Timothy understand how to behave. Just as this kind of farmer should be first to share in the fruits, so Timothy will be first to receive rewards if he works hard to serve Jesus.

Here Paul implies that other people will share in the fruits, but the farmer is one who should share in them first. In other words, he is the one who deserves to receive the benefits of his work before anyone else does.
2:7: Here Paul means that Timothy should Think about what Paul has written about soldiers, athletes, and farmers (2:4–6). He wants Timothy to apply these examples to himself as he serves Jesus.

Here the phrase in everything could refer to: (1) everything related to the three examples that Paul has given to Timothy in the previous verses; (2) everything that Timothy needs to know to serve Jesus well.
2:8: Here the word Remember indicates that Timothy should think consistently about Jesus Christ. It does not imply that Timothy might completely forget about Jesus Christ.
ἐγηγερμένον ἐκ νεκρῶν, ἐκ σπέρματος Δαυείδ
Jesus was born from the seed of David before he was raised from the dead.
Here the word raised refers to someone who died coming back to life.
Here Paul speaks as if Jesus were a plant that grew from a seed that came from David. He means that Jesus is a descendant of David.
2:9: Paul is saying that he is being treated like a criminal because he has been put in jail with those who break laws.
ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ οὐ δέδεται

Here Paul speaks as if the word of God could have been bound, as Paul has been. However, even when Paul is in jail and cannot preach the gospel in many places, the word of God cannot be restrained or contained in one place.
Here, word represents the gospel, which people communicate using words.
2:10: Paul says all here as an overstatement to emphasize that he endures every bad thing that happens to him.

Here Paul uses the spatial metaphor in Christ Jesus to describe the union of believers with Christ Jesus. In this case, being in Christ Jesus, or united to Christ Jesus, is the only way in which believers obtain salvation.
Here the phrase with eternal glory could refer to glory: (1) that goes along with salvation; (2) that characterizes salvation.
2:11: Here, word represents what Paul is about to write using words.
Here Paul refers to how believers, in their union with Christ, share in Christ’s death. In this way, they too have died.

Here Paul refers to the new life that believers receive in their union with Christ. This new life can be experienced now, but Paul seems especially to be speaking about the eternal life that believers will have after Jesus comes back.
2:12: Here Paul implies that believers must endure suffering and persecution.
Here Paul refers to people denying that they know and believe in Jesus.
Here Paul implies that at the final judgment Jesus will deny that these people know him and believe in him.
2:13: Here the word unfaithful could refer to: (1) failing to be loyal to Jesus and disobeying him; (2) failing to believe in Jesus.

Here the word faithful could indicate that: (1) Jesus remains loyal to these people. In other words, he still does what he said he would, even if they do not; (2) Jesus consistently acts based on who he is. In this case, Jesus will be faithful to his promise to deny those who deny him.
Here the phrase deny himself refers to a person choosing not to do what they would naturally do. Here, then, Paul means that Jesus is able to do only what he would naturally do.
2:14: Here Paul implies that Timothy should Remind the believers who are with him and over whom he has responsibility.
Here the phrase these things refer to what Paul has previously written. This includes the trustworthy word in 2:11–13 and perhaps also 2:1–10.

Here Paul could be: (1) indicating that God knows and approves what Timothy should command the believers; (2) asking Timothy to put the believers under oath, making them swear by God, that they will do what Timothy tells them to do.
Here Paul refers to arguments about what words mean as if they were battles.
Here Paul implies that battling about words damages the faith of the ones hearing and stops their spiritual growth.
2:15: σπούδασον σεαυτὸν, δόκιμον παραστῆσαι τῷ Θεῷ
Here Paul means that Timothy should Strive to be the kind of person who is approved by God.
Here Paul speaks as if Timothy were a skilled worker. He means that Timothy works for God as a teacher and leader.
Paul refers to the word of truth as if it were wood or cloth that Timothy should cut straight. He means that Timothy should understand and teach the word of truth carefully and properly.
Here, word represents the gospel, which people communicate with words.
2:16: Here Paul implies that the sayings are empty of useful or true information.

Here Paul speaks of people who speak the profane empty sayings as if they could physically advance further or progress in a certain direction, and he speaks of ungodliness as that direction. He means that these people become more and more ungodly as they speak these sayings.
2:17: Here, word represents what people communicate using words. In this case, Paul is referring specifically to the “profane empty sayings” to which he referred in 2:16.
Paul is saying that profane empty sayings will spread like gangrene because both these sayings and gangrene spread quickly and are dangerous.

The word gangrene refers to a type of tissue death caused by infection or lack of blood circulation. The type of gangrene that Paul is referring to can spread quickly through a person’s body and can lead to death.
The words Hymenaeus and Philetus are names of men.
2:18: Paul speaks as if the truth were a mark or target that these two men have missed. Paul means that these men have failed to maintain the truth.
Here Paul speaks of faith as if it were an object that these two men could overturn. He means that they are disrupting or destroying people’s faith in Jesus.
2:19: ὁ … στερεὸς θεμέλιος τοῦ Θεοῦ ἕστηκεν

Here Paul speaks of a firm foundation that stands to indicate that something that God has established is secure and will remain. Paul could be referring to: (1) God’s people, the church. In this case, God has established his people as a firm foundation, and no false teaching can make them stop believing; (2) the gospel. In this case, God has established the gospel as a firm foundation, and no false teaching can corrupt it.

Here Paul speaks as if the foundation had a seal on it. He means that God has made official statements about the foundation. These official statements guarantee that the foundation is valid and belongs to God.
Here the word Lord could refer to: (1) Jesus specifically; (2) God generally.
Here Paul speaks of unrighteousness if it were a location from which people should depart. He means that these people should stop doing what is unrighteous.
Here the phrase naming the name of the Lord refers to claiming that one serves and believes in the Lord.
2:20: To teach Timothy, Paul speaks of the church as if it were a great house that contained containers, which represent people who are part of the church.
The word translated as container is a general term for items that people use when they are performing household duties. These items include bowls and pots but also tools such as knives and shovels.
2:21: Here Paul continues to speak of believers as if they were each a container. In this verse, Paul gives some explanation of this figure of speech. When people cleanse themselves, they become like clean containers that can be used in honorable ways and that are useful to the master of the house, who represents God.

Here the word these could refer to: (1) what Paul has said in 2:16–18 about what the false teachers do and say. The particular focus, then, is on ungodliness and false teaching; (2) the containers for dishonor that Paul mentioned in 2:20. In this case, the focus could be on the containers or the dishonor.
2:22: Paul speaks of youthful lusts as if they were things a person could physically run away from. He means that Timothy should always avoid these lusts.
Here Paul is referring to lusts that generally characterize youthful people.

Here the phrase with the ones calling on the Lord from a pure heart could modify: (1) pursue. In this case, Timothy is supposed to pursue these good qualities along with the people who are calling on the Lord from a pure heart; (2) peace. In this case, the people with whom Timothy should have peace are those calling on the Lord from a pure heart.
Paul speaks of righteousness and other good qualities as if they were things that a person could pursue and catch. He means that Timothy should try very hard to be characterized by these good things.
Here the word faith could refer to: (1) belief in Jesus; (2) faithfulness in doing what God requires.
The phrase calling on the Lord refers to worshiping and praying to the Lord.
Here the phrase from a clean heart could be: (1) another description of these people; (2) a description of how they are calling on the Lord.
In Paul’s culture, the heart is the place where humans think and feel.
2:23: The terms foolish and ignorant mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
Here Paul speaks of the controversies as if they were mothers giving birth to children, the battles. He means that these controversies cause the battles.
Here Paul speaks of strife and quarrels within a community as if they were battles.
2:24: Here Paul speaks of people who worship and obey the Lord, and especially leaders in the church, as if they were each a slave of the Lord.
Here Paul speaks of arguing and quarreling in a community as if it were battling.
2:25: Here Paul could be implying that these people are opposing: (1) the “slave of the Lord” (2:24); (2) the gospel.
μήποτε δώῃ αὐτοῖς ὁ Θεὸς μετάνοιαν
Here Paul speaks of repentance as if it were an object that God could give people. He means that God may enable these people to have repentance.
2:26: These people must have been captured by the devil before they could become sober again from the trap of the devil.
ἀνανήψωσιν ἐκ τῆς τοῦ διαβόλου παγίδος
Here Paul implies that being sober again also means escaping from the trap of the devil.
Here Paul speaks of being able to think clearly about what is true as if it were becoming sober again.
ἐκ τῆς τοῦ διαβόλου παγίδος, ἐζωγρημένοι ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ
Here Paul speaks of how the devil has gained power or control over these people as if he had captured them in a trap.
3:1: Here the phrase last days refers to the period of time before Jesus comes back. Christians have different understandings about whether Paul believed that this time period had already begun or would begin sometime in the future.
Here Paul implies that the times will be difficult for believers because of what other people do and say that may harm or injure them (see 3:2–5).
3:2: Here the phrase lovers of self refers people who love themselves more than they love other people.
3:4: Here Paul speaks of proud people as if it they were puffed up by air.
3:5: Here the phrase a form of godliness refers to the appearance of godliness. In other words, these people appear to be acting in godly ways.

Here Paul implies that these people refuse to experience and act upon the power that comes with real godliness. In other words, they do not actually do what is godly, and they do not allow God to change them so that they become more godly.
Here Paul speaks of avoiding people as if it were done by turning away from them.
3:6: Here Paul is referring to how these people visit other people’s homes. The word translated entering implies that these people used false pretenses and deception to visit these homes.
Here Paul speaks about how these people influence little women as if they were taking these women captive. He means that they gain control and power over these women.

Here Paul refers to the women who are deceived by the false teachers as if they were physically little. He could mean that: (1) these women are spiritually weak and immature; (2) gullible or easily deceived.
Paul speaks of these women’s sins as if they were heaped on their backs. He could mean that: (1) these women sin often or even continually; (2) these women feel terrible guilt because of their sins.
Paul speaks about these various desires as if they could physically lead the women away. He means that these women do whatever they desire without trying to control themselves.
3:7: μηδέποτε εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν ἀληθείας ἐλθεῖν δυνάμενα
Here Paul speaks of the knowledge of the truth as if it were a destination at which people could arrive. He is indicating that these women cannot gain the knowledge of the truth.
3:8: Here Paul refers to something that happened when God sent Moses to tell Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, to set the Israelites free. When Moses performed a miracle, some of the magicians and sorcerers who served Pharaoh also performed that miracle. In this way, they tried to prevent Moses from doing what God had told him to do. While the names of these magicians are not mentioned in the story in Exodus, their traditional names are Jannes and Jambres.
The words Jannes and Jambres are names of men.
Here Paul implies that, when God tests the faith of these people, he will not approve of it.
Here the word faith could refer to: (1) the act of having faith in Jesus; (2) what people believe about Jesus when they have faith in him.
3:9: Here the word But introduces what will happen to these false teachers in contrast to what they are trying to do, which is to oppose the truth.
Here Paul speaks of people having success in teaching as if they were advancing further in a direction. He means that these people will cease to have success in teaching.
Paul says all here as an overstatement for emphasis.

Here Paul is referring to how Pharaoh’s magicians failed to oppose Moses. They could not copy some of the miracles that Moses did (see Exodus 8:18–19), and they were affected by other miracles that Moses did (see Exodus 9:11). In that way, everyone realized that they were foolish.
3:10: Here Paul speaks as if Timothy followed the things that Paul has done and experienced. He means that Timothy has paid attention to these things and imitates how Paul does and experiences them.
3:11: Here the phrase such as could refer back to: (1) just the sufferings; (2) both the sufferings and the persecutions.

Here the phrase what kind of persecutions I endured could be: (1) a further definition of what Paul experienced in the three cities to which he has referred; (2) an explanation that indicates how much Paul experienced.
3:12: Here Paul uses the spatial metaphor in Christ Jesus to describe the union of believers with Christ Jesus. In this case, being in Christ Jesus, or united to Christ Jesus, is how believers live godly.
3:13: Here the phrase evil men and impostors could: (1) refer to two different groups of people; (2) describe one group of people using two terms connected with and.

Here Paul speaks of these people as if they could physically advance or progress in a certain direction, and he speaks of the worse as that direction. He means that these people become worse and worse.
Here Paul speaks as if the evil men and impostors could literally lead people astray and be led astray. He means that they will deceive others and be deceived themselves.
3:14: Here Paul speaks as if what Timothy learned and was convinced of were places in which Timothy could remain. He means that Timothy should continue to believe and trust those things.
Here Paul implies that Timothy knows that these people are trustworthy.
3:15: Here Paul uses the spatial metaphor in Christ Jesus to describe the union of believers with Christ. In this case, being in Christ Jesus, or united to Christ Jesus, explains how Timothy can have faith.
3:16: Here Paul speaks as if God had breathed all Scripture. He means that God is the one who spoke or gave Scripture through his Spirit. In other words, All Scripture has its origin in God.
Here the phrase translated as All Scripture refers to what we call the Old Testament. Paul could be referring to: (1) the entirety of Scripture; (2) each of the individual scriptures.
Here Paul could be implying that Scripture is profitable: (1) for someone to use in the following ways; (2) as it functions in the following ways for those who read or hear it.
3:17: ἄρτιος … πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἐξηρτισμένος
The terms complete and equipped for every good work mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
4:1: Here Paul could be: (1) indicating that God and Christ Jesus know and approve what Paul is about to write. Also, he means that he is as sure about what he is about to write as he is sure about Jesus’ appearing and kingdom; (2) putting Timothy under oath, making him swear by God and Christ Jesus, that he will do what Paul is about to write. Also, he wants Timothy to be as sure about doing what Paul is about to write as Timothy is sure about Jesus’ appearing and kingdom.
Many ancient manuscripts read and by his appearing.
Here the phrase his appearing refers to when Jesus will come back to this world, which is when he will judge everyone.
4:2: Here, word represents the gospel, which people communicate using words.
Here Paul speaks as if Timothy should stand by something. He could mean that Timothy: (1) should be ready or prepared to preach the gospel; (2) should be persistent in preaching the gospel.
Here Paul could be implying that it will be opportune sometimes and inopportune sometimes for: (1) Timothy’s audience; (2) Timothy.
Here the words patience and teaching could: (1) describe two separate things; (2) refer to one thing described with two words connected by and.
4:3: Here the phrase bear with refers to listening to something charitably. Paul means that these people no longer be willing to listen to the healthy teaching.
Here Paul speaks as if teaching could be healthy. He means that this teaching is good and reliable in every way and has no defect or corruption.
Paul speaks of how these people gather many teachers as if they were heaping these teachers up in a pile. Paul implies that these teachers teach many different things that are wrong.

Here Paul speaks as if these people had an ear that was itching, and the only way to scratch the itch was to hear what they wanted to hear. He means that these people want to hear things that make them feel good about themselves.
4:4: ἀπὸ … τῆς ἀληθείας τὴν ἀκοὴν ἀποστρέψουσιν
Paul speaks about people no longer paying attention as if they were physically turning their ears away so that they could not hear.
Here Paul speaks about people paying attention to myths as if someone were getting them to turn away in the wrong direction.

The word myths refers to a certain kind of story that is generally considered to be untrustworthy. This kind of story is often about what important people did a long time ago. Often, many people in a culture know these stories but do not consider them to be reliable historical narratives.
4:5: Here Paul speaks as if he wants Timothy to avoid getting drunk so that he is sober. While Paul did write that Christians should not get drunk (see Ephesians 5:18), here he primarily means that Timothy should control himself and be alert.
4:6: Here Paul describes himself as if he were the wine that people in his culture would pour on a sacrifice before they offered it to God. He means that he is experiencing the final days of his life, and both these days and his death will honor God.
Paul is referring to his death in a polite way by using the phrase my departure.
4:7: Here Paul speaks about how he has persevered in believing in and obeying Jesus as if he had been a warrior fighting in a good fight or an athlete doing his best to win an event. He means that he has encountered opposition, pain, and problems, but he has persisted and persevered in believing in and obeying Jesus.
Here the phrase the good fight could indicate: (1) that the fight is right or just; (2) that someone is fighting well.
Here Paul speaks of how he has served God as if it were a race that he has now finished. He means that he has served God well, and now his time of service is about to end, since he will soon die.
Here Paul speaks of the faith as if it were a valuable object that he has kept safe. He means that he has preserved and protected the faith.
Here the word faith could refer to: (1) the act of having faith in Jesus; (2) what Christians believe about Jesus when they have faith in him; (3) the act of being faithful.
4:8: Here the word translated as From now on could introduce: (1) something that is true from that moment and into the future; (2) the last thing that Paul wants to say about how he has lived his life.
Here Paul describes the reward that he expects to receive as if it were the crown that athletes in his culture received when they won an event.
Here Paul is referring to the exact moment when Jesus will return to this world, which will also be the end of the current time period. This will be the time when Jesus judges everyone.
πᾶσιν τοῖς ἠγαπηκόσι τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν αὐτοῦ
Here the phrase having loved his appearing indicates that these people care about, long for, and rejoice at his appearing.
Here the phrase his appearing refers to when Jesus will come back to this world, which is when he will act as a judge.
4:10: The words Demas and Crescens are names of men.

Here the phrase the present age refers to the time period in which Paul and Timothy lived, the time period before Jesus comes back and God transforms everything. Here Paul implies that Demas loves what he can have and experience during this time period.
The word Dalmatia is the name of a Roman province on the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea. This area is now part of the countries Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina.
4:11: Here Paul could be implying that Mark is useful: (1) in helping Paul minister to others, especially by preaching and teaching; (2) in helping Paul to take care of his personal needs.
4:13: The term cloak refers to a heavy garment that was worn over other clothes.
Here the phrase especially the parchments could indicate: (1) that some of the scrolls are especially important to Paul; (2) that the scrolls that Paul wants are the parchments.
The word parchments refers to documents written on specially treated animal skins.
4:14: A coppersmith is a person who makes things out of copper and other metals.
The word Alexander is the name of a man.
Here Paul means that Alexander did many evil things to him.
Here Paul speaks of how the Lord will punish Alexander as if the Lord were repaying Alexander for his works.
4:15: Here, words represents the message that Paul and the people with him proclaimed using words.
4:16: Here the phrase first defense refers to the first time that Paul was in court and had to defend himself against accusations. Paul implies that he already had appeared in court again or that he would have to do so again in the future.

Here Paul means that no one went with Paul to the court to help him defend himself. They might have been able to help Paul by testifying that he had not done anything wrong, or they might have just sat in the court to show that they approved of Paul.
Here Paul means that he does not want his fellow believers to be punished for not appearing with him in court. He uses this form as a way to ask God to forgive them for forsaking him.
4:17: Here Paul speaks as if the Lord had physically stood with him. He means that the Lord supported and helped him.

Here Paul may mean that the proclamation was fulfilled: (1) because he was able to proclaim the good news in every place and way that God required of him; (2) because he proclaimed the entire gospel message.
Paul says all here as an overstatement for emphasis.

Here Paul speaks as if he was about to be eaten by a lion when he was rescued out of the mouth of that lion. He means that he was protected from terrible danger, which was most likely the danger of being executed.
4:18: Here the phrase forever {and} ever identifies an action that will never end, and it strongly emphasizes that it will never end.
4:19: Here Paul asks Timothy to extend greetings for him to other people that both he and the Timothy know. See the chapter introduction for more information.
4:20: The words Erastus and Trophimus are the names of men.
The name Miletus is the name of a city on the western coast of what is now Turkey, south of Ephesus.
4:21: Where Paul and Timothy lived, winter is the time of year when it is cold and travel is difficult.
Here Paul extends greetings from people who are with him and who know the person to whom he is writing, Timothy. See the chapter introduction for more information.
The words Eubulus, Pudens, and Linus are the names of three men.
The word Claudia is the name of a woman.
Here Paul refers to the brothers to include all the other believers who wanted to greet Timothy. Paul does not mean that Eubulus, Pudens, Linus, and Claudia are not brothers.
Paul is using the term brothers to mean people who share the same faith.
4:22: ὁ Κύριος μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματός σου
As was customary in his culture, Paul closes his letter with a blessing for Timothy.
Paul is using spirit to represent Timothy as a whole person. He may use this figure of speech to indicate that the Lord will be with Timothy in a spiritual way, not a physical way.
As was customary in his culture, Paul closes his letter with a blessing for Timothy and the believers with him. He implies that the Grace is from God.
Because Paul gives this blessing to Timothy and all the believers who are with him, this is the only place in the letter where you is plural.
Many ancient manuscripts read you. Other ancient manuscripts read “you.
